text: Crystalline-Silicon Modules Trends in U.S. module imports by origin region during 2020–2024 are shown in Figure 10. The United States imported 45.9 GW of c-Si modules in 2024, which was only 0.4 GW more than dc dc in 2023 but up 100% from 2022. However, module imports in Q4 2024 were 52% lower than quarterly average imports during Q1–Q3 2024, coinciding with growth in U.S. module production. In 2024, 89% of modules imported into the United States came from Vietnam, Thailand, Cambodia, Malaysia, and the remaining countries within ASEAN—up from 77% in 2023. Despite imported modules from India contracting 32%, year over year, India was still the fifth- leading source of imports into the United States, having grown fourfold since 2022 and fortyfold since 2021. Additionally, some modules from India may be incorrectly categorized as thin-film modules, which would imply a reduction in c-Si module imports from India of only 6%.12 In contrast to China’s share of capacity shown in Figure 5, U.S. imports from China declined from less than 7% in Q1 2020 to near zero by the end of 2024. The direct trade of PV modules, cells, wafers, and polysilicon from China to the United States is affected by Section 301 tariffs and comparatively high AD/CVD rates vs. other countries. Data source: (Feldman, Zuboy, Dummit, Stright, et al. 2025) The United States has imported most of its c-Si modules from ASEAN for more than 5 years due to those countries’ low labor costs and proximity to the large and established PV supply chain in China, which can provide training, manufacturing equipment, and materials. India became a significant source in 2022, with a relatively new local PV production base and manufacturing costs to similar to ASEAN’s. Of the 45.9 GW of 2024 imports shown in Figure 10, at least 37 dc GW from ASEAN would be subject in 2025 to pending AD/CVD decisions and new duty rates dc set by the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative, U.S. International Trade Commission, and U.S. Department of Commerce.
